title: 7 Best Basement Waterproofing Products in 2026: Wall Sealers
metaDescription: DRYLOK Extreme, rated for 15 psi, is the best basement wall sealer for damp block or concrete. 7 waterproofing products matched to your leak type.
h1: The 7 Best Basement Wall Sealers and Waterproofing Products in 2026
intro:
The best basement waterproofing product for most damp block or concrete walls is DRYLOK Extreme, a masonry waterproofer rated for 15 psi of hydrostatic pressure when it is scrubbed into bare masonry. If your walls are bare poured concrete you want to leave looking untouched, a penetrating sealer like RadonSeal Plus is the better match.

Wall sealers look interchangeable on the shelf, and that is where most bad buys start. A coating that dries a sweating wall can blister off one with water pushing behind it. This guide ranks seven products by leak type, then covers how to diagnose your wall, how much to buy, prep, application, cost and when a sealer is the wrong fix.
quickAnswer: Buy DRYLOK Extreme for damp or seeping bare block and concrete, and brush the first coat in hard. Choose RadonSeal Plus for unpainted poured concrete, a liquid rubber for walls with moving hairline cracks, and Xypex for poured walls that warrant a permanent professional treatment. If water runs or pools, fix drainage before you buy any coating.

sections.heading: Basement Waterproofing Products: The Short Answer
sections.body:
**Short answer:** DRYLOK Extreme is the wall sealer to buy for most basements. Pick by how the water shows up on your wall, not by the brand.

| Pick | Best for | Key spec |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DRYLOK Extreme | Damp or seeping bare block and concrete | Acrylic-cement coating, 15 psi label rating |
| RadonSeal Plus | Bare poured concrete, no film wanted | Reactive silicate penetrant |
| DRYLOK Original | Damp walls without real water pressure | Acrylic-cement coating, 10 psi label rating |
| Liquid Rubber Foundation | Exterior walls and crack-prone damp walls | Elastomeric membrane |
| Ames Block and Wall | Block with hairline cracks | Flexible block coating |
| Xypex Concentrate | Poured concrete, water from either side | Crystalline cement slurry |
| Flex Seal Liquid | Spot repairs and pipe penetrations | Rubber coating, no pressure rating |

The psi numbers are the makers' label figures. Products without one simply do not publish a hydrostatic rating.

A sealer handles dampness and slow seepage. It does not stop a basement that floods, water rising at the floor joint or a wall that is cracking from soil pressure. Those need drainage or structural work first, which our guide to [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/) explains.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Basement Wall Sealers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
The order reflects what each maker publishes (pressure rating, coverage, cure and recoat times, surface rules), how well each chemistry suits poured concrete versus hollow block, and complaints and praise that recur in owner feedback. No product here went through lab trials for this guide; maker claims are credited as such.

### Best Overall: DRYLOK Extreme Masonry Waterproofer

DRYLOK Extreme is a heavy latex masonry waterproofer, and its label lists resistance to 15 psi of hydrostatic pressure, the top figure in the DRYLOK line and more than most below-grade walls ever see. That rating assumes the coating actually fills the pores, so the label tells you to scrub the first coat in with a nylon brush until no pinholes remain. Owners who follow that step commonly report dry walls through wet seasons; those who roll on a thin first coat often report pinhole leaks.

It is approved for poured concrete and block, inside or out, above or below grade, as long as the surface is bare. The dried film includes a mildewcide, it cleans up with water and it can be tinted to light colors at many stores. Coverage is the catch: roughly 75 to 100 square feet per gallon for the first coat on smooth concrete and less on rough block, so buy extra and favor five-gallon pails.

**Pros:** 15 psi label rating; fills block pores; mildewcide in the film; water cleanup; tintable.

**Cons:** needs bare, clean masonry; low first-coat coverage; tiring to brush in properly.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DRYLOK+Extreme+Masonry+Waterproofer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Penetrating Sealer: RadonSeal Plus

RadonSeal Plus works the opposite way from a masonry paint. This water-based silicate sealer soaks into poured concrete and reacts with the free lime inside to form a gel that blocks the capillaries below the surface. The maker says it penetrates several inches into dense concrete.

With no film on the face of the wall, there is nothing for water pressure or salt deposits to push off, and the wall looks exactly as it did before. That suits owners who like the plain concrete look or plan to leave walls exposed. The limits are clear, though. It needs unpainted, unsealed concrete that can absorb it, it does less on hollow block than on solid poured walls, and it carries no psi rating, so treat it as a way to cut dampness and seepage rather than a dam. Because nothing visible changes, judging results takes a wet season or two.

**Pros:** no film to peel or blister; invisible finish; reduces water and vapor movement; treats walls and slabs.

**Cons:** needs bare concrete; no pressure rating; results are slow to judge.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=RadonSeal+Plus+penetrating+concrete+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget: DRYLOK Original Masonry Waterproofer

DRYLOK Original is the older formula in the same family, and many basements need nothing more. The label lists 10 psi of hydrostatic pressure, below Extreme but still well above what a typical residential wall with working gutters faces. Application is identical: stir thoroughly, scrub the first coat into bare masonry, and add a second once it dries.

The practical difference is margin. For a wall that is merely damp, sweats in summer or shows a dark band near the floor after storms, Original does the job for less. For seepage lines or wet patches that spread, Extreme's higher rating is the safer purchase. Both share the same weakness: paint, salt crust or mold left under the coating shortens its life.

**Pros:** 10 psi label rating; usually cheaper per gallon than Extreme; white and tintable bases; same proven method.

**Cons:** lower rating; same demanding prep; hard brushing on the first coat.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DRYLOK+Original+Masonry+Waterproofer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Exterior Walls: Liquid Rubber Foundation and Basement Sealant

Liquid Rubber cures into a thick, stretchy membrane, and that flexibility is what rigid coatings lack. Freeze-thaw cycles open and close hairline cracks, which can tear a stiff masonry paint, while an elastomeric coat built to the recommended thickness stretches over the movement.

That makes it a strong choice on the outside of a foundation while the soil is dug back, since water pressure on that side presses the membrane into the wall instead of off it. Indoors it handles damp and condensation-prone block well, though owners sometimes report bubbles where water pushes from behind, the usual limit of any rubber film on the inside face. It is water-based, low in odor and brushes, rolls or sprays. Thick coats mean low coverage, so price the whole job before you start.

**Pros:** bridges hairline cracks; water-based and low odor; suits exterior excavation work; brush, roll or spray.

**Cons:** low coverage per gallon; can bubble on pressurized interior walls; costly over large areas.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Liquid+Rubber+Foundation+and+Basement+Sealant&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Block Cracks: Ames Block and Wall

Ames Block and Wall is a water-based elastomeric coating formulated for concrete block and other masonry. Like other liquid rubbers, its cured film stretches over hairline and shrinkage cracks instead of splitting along them, which helps on older block foundations with slightly opened mortar joints. Ames generally calls for several coats to build full film thickness, and the cured coating can be painted.

It is a weaker fit for an interior wall with water actively pushing through, because a flexible film on the inside face can lift and blister under steady pressure; a cement-based waterproofer is safer there. It shines on exterior block, garage walls, retaining walls and basements with mild seepage and cracking. Prep is the same as any coating: clean, sound, dry and free of salt crust.

**Pros:** flexes with small crack movement; made for block; soap-and-water cleanup; paintable once cured.

**Cons:** not for strong pressure from inside; needs multiple coats; harder to find locally.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ames+Block+and+Wall+liquid+rubber&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Poured Concrete: Xypex Concentrate

Xypex Concentrate is the professional product on this list. It is a dry powder of cement, fine sand and proprietary chemicals that you mix into a slurry and brush onto concrete that has been prepped and soaked. The active chemicals migrate into the concrete and react with moisture to grow insoluble crystals in pores and hairline cracks, and the company says those crystals can reactivate when water returns.

Because it becomes part of the concrete, it works against water from the inside face, which is why it shows up in elevator pits and water tanks. It is also unforgiving: the surface must be open-textured and saturated, the slurry mixed and applied at the specified rate, and the coat kept moist while it cures. It is designed for poured concrete, not hollow block. Follow the technical data sheet to the letter or hire an approved applicator.

**Pros:** crystals self-seal hairline cracks when wet; works from either side; becomes part of the concrete; long record below grade.

**Cons:** exacting mixing and prep; plain gray finish; best results from trained applicators.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Xypex+Concentrate+crystalline+waterproofing&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Spot Repairs: Flex Seal Liquid

Plenty of people search for Flex Seal basement waterproofing, and the product does have a job in a basement. It is a thick rubber coating that brushes onto almost any material and cures to a flexible, watertight skin. That is useful around pipe penetrations, window well seams, the outside face of a cracked foundation at grade and small spots where different materials meet.

As a whole-wall sealer it is the weakest pick here. It is not designed to fill block pores, it has no hydrostatic rating for use on the inside face, and its cost per square foot is high next to a masonry waterproofer. The solvent formula also smells strong indoors. Owner feedback is generally positive for patches and disappointed for full walls, which fits the design.

**Pros:** sold almost everywhere; thick coat for small patches; bonds to many materials; handy for penetrations.

**Cons:** poor value for whole walls; no masonry pressure rating; solvent odor.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Flex+Seal+Liquid+rubber+sealant&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Is Your Basement Wall Wet From Condensation or Seepage?
sections.body:
Tape an 18-inch square of clear plastic to the bare wall, seal all four edges, and check it after a day or two. Water on the room side means condensation; water between the plastic and the masonry means seepage. This is the idea behind ASTM D4263, the moisture check coating makers reference, and it answers the most important question before you spend anything.

### Moisture on the room side

Droplets on the outside of the sheet come from humid basement air hitting a cool wall. A sealer cannot fix that, because the water never came through the concrete. A dehumidifier is the right tool; see our [basement dehumidifier picks](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/).

### Moisture behind the plastic

Water trapped against the wall is wicking through from the soil, and that is exactly what a wall sealer is for. Other signs agree: a dark band along the lowest foot of wall, white crusty salt deposits, or a crack that weeps after heavy rain. A steady trickle or a spurt from a tie hole is a different category. That is water under pressure, and it needs plugging and drainage before any coating will stay on.

### Watch the timing

Condensation peaks in muggy summer weather on the coolest stretch of wall and fades once the heat comes on. Seepage follows rain and snowmelt, appears a day or two after a storm and lingers at the base of the wall. A few weeks of notes usually make the pattern obvious.

### Write down three facts before you shop

Poured concrete or hollow block? Bare or painted? Damp, seeping or running at worst? Those three answers narrow seven products to one or two in a minute.

sections.heading: What Types of Basement Wall Sealer Are There?
sections.body:
There are four families: cement-latex masonry waterproofers, penetrating sealers, elastomeric liquid rubbers and crystalline slurries. The family tells you more about how a can will behave than the brand does.

### Masonry waterproofers

Products like DRYLOK are thick, solids-heavy coatings. Scrubbed into the surface, they plug block and concrete pores and leave a film that resists water from behind. They change the look of the wall and bond only to bare, clean masonry. For a seeping interior block wall, start here.

### Penetrating sealers

Silicates such as RadonSeal densify concrete by filling capillaries; silane-siloxane repellents make pore walls shed water. Neither leaves a film, so nothing peels and the wall looks unchanged. Both need an unpainted surface that can absorb them.

### Elastomeric liquid rubbers

Liquid Rubber and Ames cure into a stretchy membrane that spans hairline cracks as they open and close. They work best outside, or on interior walls that are damp rather than pressurized, because a rubber film pushed from behind will bubble.

### Crystalline slurries

Xypex and similar products are cement slurries with chemicals that grow crystals inside concrete whenever water is present. They suit poured walls, need a saturated surface and careful mixing, and punish shortcuts.

| Type | Best surface | Handles pressure? | Changes the look? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry waterproofer | Bare block or concrete | Yes, to the labeled psi | Yes, paint-like |
| Silicate penetrant | Bare poured concrete | Reduces seepage, no rating | No |
| Silane-siloxane | Bare block or concrete | Repels only | No |
| Elastomeric rubber | Exterior or damp interior | Limited on the inside face | Yes, thick membrane |
| Crystalline | Poured concrete | Yes, when applied correctly | Yes, gray cement |

sections.heading: What Does a Hydrostatic Pressure Rating Mean?
sections.body:
It is the water pressure a film coating withstood from behind in the maker's test: 10 psi for DRYLOK Original and 15 psi for DRYLOK Extreme. Water in saturated soil adds roughly 0.43 psi for each foot of depth, so a wall with the water table 8 feet up sees about 3.5 psi at its base. The ratings look generous, but they come from a lab sample, not your wall.

### Which products carry one

Only film coatings designed to stay bonded under back pressure. Interior elastomerics usually list none, and penetrating sealers cannot, since there is no film to push off. Use the figure to choose between two film coatings, not as a guarantee.

### What the rating leaves out

No wall coating stops water entering at the cove joint where wall meets slab, water pouring through a crack, or water rising through the floor. If water shows up in those places, drainage is the main fix.

| Number | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 15 psi | DRYLOK Extreme label rating |
| 10 psi | DRYLOK Original label rating |
| 0.43 psi | Added per foot of water depth |
| 28 days | Typical cure before coating new concrete |

sections.heading: How Much Basement Wall Sealer Do You Need?
sections.body:
Plan on 18 to 24 gallons of masonry waterproofer for two coats on 1,000 square feet of wall. That is far more than paint, because the first coat disappears into the pores.

### Measure the wall, not the floor

Multiply the basement perimeter by the height of exposed wall, then subtract big openings. A 30-by-40-foot basement has 140 feet of perimeter; at 7.5 feet of bare wall that is about 1,050 square feet. Walkout walls and finished sections cut the number quickly.

### Coverage by product type

DRYLOK lists about 75 to 100 square feet per gallon for the first coat on smooth concrete, less on rough block, and better coverage on the second coat. For 1,050 square feet, budget 11 to 14 gallons for coat one and 8 to 10 for coat two. Penetrating sealers vary with how thirsty the concrete is, and liquid rubbers go on thick.

| Product type | Typical coverage per gallon | Coats | Gallons for 1,000 sq ft |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry waterproofer | 75 to 100 sq ft (first coat) | 2 | 18 to 24 |
| Silicate penetrant | 150 to 250 sq ft | 1 to 2 | 4 to 10 |
| Silane-siloxane | 100 to 200 sq ft | 1 | 5 to 10 |
| Liquid rubber | 50 to 75 sq ft per coat | 2 to 3 | 30 to 50 |

### Buy it all at once

A wall left half-coated for three days while you wait for another gallon ends up with a lap line, and in a film coating that cold joint is a weak spot. Buy for the low end of the coverage range and return unopened containers.

sections.heading: How Do You Prep and Apply a Basement Wall Sealer?
sections.body:
Get the wall to clean, bare, sound masonry, then brush the first coat in hard, let it dry, add a second coat and hunt pinholes with a light. Prep decides whether the coating is still there in five years.

### Strip paint and remove salt

Most masonry waterproofers and every penetrating sealer need bare masonry to perform as labeled, so scrape and wire-brush old paint. Efflorescence, the white salt crust left as water evaporates, must be brushed off dry, washed with a masonry cleaner or concrete etch and rinsed. Coating over it is the top reason basement coatings flake within a year.

### Patch cracks and kill mold

The coating can fill hairline cracks. Anything wider than about 1/8 inch needs a masonry patch or polyurethane crack sealant, and an actively leaking hole needs hydraulic cement, which expands as it sets. Clean any mold with a labeled product; our [mold killer guide](/best-mold-remover/) covers which to use on concrete. Let the wall dry, and keep surface and air above 50 degrees Fahrenheit through the cure.

### Stir, brush, then recoat

Stir to the bottom of the can, never shake, and restir every 15 minutes. Use a stiff nylon masonry brush for the first coat, working small sections until no pinholes show. Once it has dried for the label time, apply the second coat; a 3/4-inch nap roller is acceptable on smooth poured concrete, but stay with a brush on block. Then hold a work light flat to the wall and dab every pinhole that glows.

### Details that matter

Cut in around pipes, boxes and the sill with a small brush, mask wood framing, and carry the coating a few inches onto the slab so the cove joint is covered. Ventilate throughout, and with solvent products, mind pilot lights and the furnace if the label warns of flammable vapor.

sections.heading: Should You Waterproof Basement Walls From the Inside or Outside?
sections.body:
Exterior waterproofing is better engineering; interior sealing is what most homeowners can afford. So do the cheap outside fixes, then seal the inside carefully.

### Why outside wins

An interior coating sits on the negative side, where water arrives through the wall and pushes it off. An exterior membrane sits on the positive side, where pressure presses it into the wall. The cost of that advantage is excavation.

### The cheap outside fixes come first

Extend downspouts several feet from the foundation, regrade so soil falls away from the house (residential code calls for 6 inches of drop over the first 10 feet where possible), and keep gutters clean. These cut the water reaching the wall and make an interior coating far more likely to last.

### When excavation is worth it

When soil stays saturated, when walls are bowing or cracking structurally, or when you are digging anyway. A pro then applies a membrane, drainage board and footing drain. Our guide to [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/) compares that with an interior drain and sump.

### A middle option for damp block

For block that is damp but not leaking, an interior silane-siloxane penetrant reduces wicking without a film that can blister. If you will paint later, read our guide to the [best paint for cinder block](/best-paint-for-cinder-block/) first, since many penetrants block paint adhesion.

sections.heading: How Much Does It Cost to Seal Basement Walls?
sections.body:
A DIY job on a 1,000-square-foot basement typically runs about $300 to $900 in coating plus $50 to $150 in brushes, cleaner and patch, while hiring it out commonly runs about $3,000 to $7,000. Materials are the cheap part.

### What contractors charge

Contractors commonly quote $3 to $7 per square foot for a cleaned, patched, two-coat interior application. Most of that is labor for scrubbing and brushing, which a patient DIYer can handle over two or three weekends.

### How it compares with drainage

A sealer is a smaller tool, not a cheaper version of the same fix. Interior perimeter drains with a sump commonly run $5,000 to $15,000, and exterior excavation with a membrane can reach $15,000 to $30,000 or more.

| Approach | Typical cost | Fixes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DIY masonry waterproofer | $300 to $900 materials | Dampness, slow seepage |
| DIY penetrating sealer | $200 to $700 materials | Wicking, dusting |
| Pro interior coating | $3,000 to $7,000 | Same, done for you |
| Interior drain plus sump | $5,000 to $15,000 | Cove joint water, high water table |
| Exterior membrane | $15,000 to $30,000+ | Saturated soil, structural repairs |

### Time as well as money

Expect a day of clearing and scrubbing, a day of patching and drying, and two separate brushing days, spread over a week or more with cure times.

sections.heading: When Should You Not Use a Basement Wall Sealer?
sections.body:
Skip the sealer when the wall is moving, when the moisture is condensation, when radon is the real concern or when the basement floods.

### The wall is cracking or bowing

Horizontal cracks in block, stair-step cracks through mortar and inward bowing point to soil pressure. A coating hides the evidence while the movement continues. Call a structural engineer first.

### The problem is a musty smell

If the plastic test showed condensation, the fix is controlling humidity in the air, not coating the wall.

### You are worried about radon

Sealing cracks can reduce soil gas entry, but EPA guidance treats sealing as a supplement to active mitigation, not a replacement. Test the air, and if it reads 4 pCi/L or higher, hire a certified mitigation contractor.

### Water pools on the floor

Water that pools after storms is coming in at the floor joint or through the slab, beyond a wall coating's reach. Install drainage and a sump first, then coat the walls if they are still damp.

mistakes.title: Brushing Over Efflorescence
mistakes.body: Salt crust left under a new film keeps growing and pushes the coating off, usually within the first year. Brush it off dry, wash with a masonry cleaner or concrete etch, rinse and let the wall dry fully. Salt that returns quickly means water is still moving through the wall.

mistakes.title: Rolling On the First Coat
mistakes.body: A roller skims across block pores instead of filling them, leaving thousands of pinholes. The first coat of any masonry waterproofer needs a stiff nylon brush worked into the surface. Save the roller for the second coat on smooth poured concrete, and inspect under a raking light.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the Cove Joint
mistakes.body: Much basement water enters where the wall meets the slab, not through the wall face. Coat the bottom few inches carefully and seal the joint with a product made for it. If water still rises along that seam, an interior drain, not a coating, is the fix.

mistakes.title: Coating Over Old Paint
mistakes.body: A waterproofer brushed over latex paint is only as strong as the paint's grip on the wall, and penetrating sealers cannot soak through paint at all. Strip or grind the old finish first, or choose an approach that does not depend on a bond to bare masonry.

mistakes.title: Sealing Before Fixing Gutters and Grading
mistakes.body: Moving roof water away from the foundation is the cheapest waterproofing any house gets. Coating the inside while a downspout dumps beside the wall is backward. Extend downspouts, regrade low spots, and coat only if the wall is still damp after a few heavy rains.

faqs.q: What is the best basement wall waterproofing sealer?
faqs.a: DRYLOK Extreme is the best basement wall waterproofing sealer for most bare block and concrete walls. It fills masonry pores and carries a 15 psi hydrostatic label rating when brushed in properly. For unpainted poured concrete that should keep its natural look, a penetrating sealer like RadonSeal Plus fits better. Neither replaces drainage where water runs in.

faqs.q: What is the best interior basement wall sealer?
faqs.a: A cement-latex masonry waterproofer such as DRYLOK Extreme is the best interior basement wall sealer, because it is built to stay bonded with water pushing from behind. Elastomeric rubbers can bubble on the inside face under pressure. Fix gutters and grading outside first so the interior coating has less water to resist.

faqs.q: Does Flex Seal work for basement waterproofing?
faqs.a: Flex Seal works for small basement patches, pipe penetrations and window well seams, but it is a poor choice for whole walls. It is not formulated to fill masonry pores, has no hydrostatic pressure rating for interior use and costs far more per square foot than DRYLOK. Use a masonry waterproofer for full walls.

faqs.q: Is one coat of basement wall sealer enough?
faqs.a: One coat is usually not enough for a masonry waterproofer. Most walls need two, with the first brushed in hard, and rough block may need a third pass over stubborn pinholes. Penetrating sealers typically need one saturating coat, sometimes a second wet-on-wet coat on porous block. Follow your product's label for recoat timing.

faqs.q: How long does basement waterproofing paint last?
faqs.a: Basement waterproofing paint typically lasts five to ten years on an interior wall before needing touch-ups, often longer on a well-prepped wall. How much water reaches the wall matters most. Early failures usually trace back to salt crust left underneath, a thin rolled first coat, or gutters and grading still sending water toward the foundation.

faqs.q: Does a basement wall sealer stop mold?
faqs.a: A basement wall sealer helps with mold only indirectly. It cuts moisture wicking through the masonry, and some waterproofers include a mildewcide in the film, but it does nothing about mold from condensation. Keep relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50 percent, with a dehumidifier to control mold.

faqs.q: Can you paint over basement wall sealer?
faqs.a: You can usually paint over a cured masonry waterproofer with latex paint, though many owners skip it because waterproofers come tinted. Painting over a penetrating sealer often fails, since silane-siloxane repellents can prevent paint from bonding. If paint is part of the plan, check the sealer's data sheet for compatibility before you buy.

bottomLine: For most damp basements, DRYLOK Extreme brushed onto clean, bare masonry is the safest single purchase: it carries a published 15 psi rating, fills block pores and is stocked nearly everywhere. RadonSeal Plus is the better fit for unpainted poured concrete you want to leave looking natural, a liquid rubber suits crack-prone walls, and Xypex is for poured walls that justify a professional treatment. Whatever you buy, the order of work matters more than the label: send roof water away from the house, scrub off the salt, patch the cracks, then coat. Done in that order, a wall sealer is money well spent; brushed over salt beside a dumping downspout, it rarely lasts a winter.
